canonicalExplanation.summary: Pick the structure for the job. **Array**: ordered list. **Object**: a record with known string keys. **Map**: key → value lookups where keys can be **any value** (objects, DOM nodes, numbers) without being turned into strings. **Set**: unique values. Both Map and Set compare keys by **identity** — two separate objects with the same contents are different keys. Copies with spread are **shallow**; use `structuredClone` for a deep copy of plain data.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
You want to remember which buttons on a page have been clicked. Using an object with the button as a key turns every button into the same string "[object HTMLButtonElement]" — all buttons collide! A Map uses a DOM node object as a key without string coercion. In this lesson you'll select and use Array, Object, Map or Set, and identify aliasing in a nested copy.

examples.title: A Map keyed by DOM nodes
examples.situation: A Map uses a DOM node object as a key without string coercion.
walkthrough: **Problem:** `counts[btn]` converts every button to the same string key, so counts collide.
**Map uses a DOM node object as a key:** `clicks.set(btn, (clicks.get(btn) ?? 0) + 1)` keeps one entry per button, without string coercion.
**Check:** clicking button A twice and B once, `clicks.get(A)` will read 2 and `clicks.get(B)` 1.
examples.result: Each button has its own click count, stored against the button itself.

examples.title: The copied course that changed the original
examples.situation: An editor makes a draft with `const draft = { ...course }`, adds a tag to `draft.tags`, then cancels — but the published course now shows the new tag.
walkthrough: Spread copied the top level; tags is the same array in both.
Pushing to draft.tags mutated course.tags too.
Fix: `const draft = structuredClone(course)` so nested arrays are independent.
examples.result: Cancelling a draft leaves the published course unchanged.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Two separate objects with identical properties are one Set value because their contents match.
misconceptions.correction: Sets and Maps compare objects by identity (same reference), not by contents. Two separate objects with equal properties are two members; use primitive keys (like an id) if you mean equal content.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why was the Set size 2?

analogy.example: A Map with object keys is like a **coat check that tags the actual coat**, not a description of it — two identical-looking coats get two different tickets. A Set is a **guest list of actual people**: twins are still two guests.
limitations: Coat checks don't copy coats; shallow copies share inner items.
structuredClone is like buying a new identical coat.

remediation.explanation: Ask: **What operation dominates — order, named fields, lookup by any key, or uniqueness?** Then, for copies: **does it contain nested objects? → structuredClone.**

recap.summary: To select and use Array, Object, Map or Set, pick by operation: order, named fields, lookup by any key type, or uniqueness. Maps and Sets use identity for object keys. Spread copies are shallow — identify aliasing in nested copies and use structuredClone when you need independence.
